title: IRC SP 88 Road Safety Audit Manual
text: IRC SP:88 Road Safety Audit Manual — Summary Issuing Body: Indian Roads Congress (IRC) Document: IRC:SP:88 2019 "Guidelines for Road Safety Audit" Applicability: All national and state highways in India, including Maharashtra 1. Purpose of Road Safety Audit A Road Safety Audit (RSA) is a formal examination of an existing or future road project to determine its potential to cause road accidents or casualties. The audit independently evaluates road safety performance using a defined checklist methodology. 2. Black Spot Identification Method (IRC) IRC recommends the following quantitative method for black spot identification: Accident Frequency Method: Sections with 5+ injury accidents in 3 years qualify as black spots. Accident Rate Method: Accident rate per vehicle kilometer traveled (VKT) above threshold triggers black spot classification. Severity Index: Weighted score = (12 × Fatal + 3 × Grievous + 1 × Simple) / Total accidents. Sites scoring 15 are high priority. 3. Road Safety Inspection Checklist (Key Items) 3.1 Geometry and Alignment Adequate sight distance at intersections and curves (min 180m stopping sight distance on highways). Transition curves at sharp bends. Adequate shoulder width (minimum 2.5m on 2 lane highways). 3.2 Road Furniture Chevron signs at curves exceeding 30° deflection. Delineators at 10m

Adequate shoulder width (minimum 2.5m on 2 lane highways). 3.2 Road Furniture Chevron signs at curves exceeding 30° deflection. Delineators at 10m spacing in curves. W beam guardrails on embankments 3m height. 3.3 Junctions Priority control signs at all intersections. Channelization islands for turning movements. Adequate sight lines cleared of vegetation. 3.4 Lighting Continuous street lighting at junctions, school zones, and pedestrian crossings. Minimum 30 lux illuminance on arterial roads. 3.5 Pedestrian Facilities Footpath continuity audit. Zebra crossings with tactile paving at 50m intervals in urban zones. At grade crossings with 2 minute gap acceptance. 4. Key Risk Factors Identified in Maharashtra Audits Based on road safety audits conducted on NH 48 (Mumbai Pune), NH 60, and SH 27 (Ahmednagar Pune): 1. Missing crash barriers on high embankment sections in Ghat zones. 2. Inadequate junction illumination on rural NH sections. 3. Poor delineation on curves at night (reflective markers missing or faded). 4. Encroachment of road shoulders by informal market stalls. 5. Absence of speed table/humps near school/hospital zones in small towns. 6. Drains blocked leading to ponding and skidding in monsoon.

title: Maharashtra Motor Vehicles Rules — Safety Provisions Summary
text: Maharashtra Motor Vehicles Rules — Road Safety Summary Source: Maharashtra Motor Vehicles Rules 1989 (Amended through 2023) Administering Authority: Maharashtra Transport Department (RTO) Enforcement Agency: Maharashtra Traffic Police 1. Licensing & Driver Competency Requirements Commercial Vehicle Drivers (HMV/Transport): Minimum 5 years experience in LMV before HMV license. Medical fitness certificate mandatory annually after age 50. Learner's License: L board display mandatory. Cannot drive on expressways. Speed limit capped at 40 km/h. High Security Registration Plates (HSRP): Mandatory for all vehicles registered in Maharashtra from 2019 onwards. 2. Traffic Violation Fine Structure (Maharashtra, 2023) 3. Maharashtra Road Safety Policy Priorities (2022 2027) 1. Vision Zero pilot program in Pune Metropolitan Region to eliminate fatal accidents by 2027. 2. Helmet enforcement — 100% helmet compliance target for all 2 wheeler riders and pillion passengers. 3. Speed cameras — Installation of 2,400 speed detection cameras across NH and SH by 2025. 4. Drunk driving enforcement — Night checking nakas operational every Friday/Saturday at 22 identified high risk zones. 5. Black spot remediation — ₹850 crore budget allocated for engineering improvements at 450 black spots (2022 2025). 4. text: 22 identified high risk zones. 5. Black spot remediation — ₹850 crore budget allocated for engineering improvements at 450 black spots (2022 2025). 4. Statistical Context (Maharashtra, 2022 2023) Maharashtra accounts for approximately 9 10% of all road accident fatalities in India, making it one of the top 5 states by fatality count. Two wheelers constitute approximately 40% of road accident fatalities in Maharashtra. Pedestrian fatalities account for 18 22% of total deaths. Peak accident hours: 6 PM – 10 PM (evening rush + reduced visibility). Peak accident months: June–September (monsoon) and December (festival/fog season). 5. Road Safety Audit Requirements All new highway projects must undergo a road safety audit at 4 stages: Feasibility, Detailed Design, Pre opening, and Post opening (within 12 months). Auditors must be IRC certified Road Safety Auditors with minimum 3 years experience. Audit reports must be submitted to NHAI/MaHa PWD within 60 days of field inspection. 6. Accident Reporting & Investigation Protocol 1. FIR Filing: Police file First Information Report (FIR) within 24 hours of fatal accident. 2. Spot Inspection: Traffic police and PWD engineers must jointly inspect fatal accident sites within 7 days. 3. MVCR Reporting: Motor Vehicle Crash Report (MVCR) filed with MoRTH

title: Road Safety Guidelines 2022 — MoRTH
text: MoRTH Guidelines for Road Safety & Identification of Black Spots (2022) Authorizing Body: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), Government of India Document Code: MoRTH/RS 2022/BS 01 Target Domain: National Highways and State Arterials Relevant State: Maharashtra (Applies nationally, referenced by MaHa PWD) 1. Definition and Protocol for Road Accident Black Spots Under MoRTH and Indian Roads Congress (IRC) standards, a Road Accident Black Spot is defined as a road stretch of about 500 meters in length in which either: 1. 5 or more fatal accidents have occurred in the preceding three calendar years, OR 2. 10 or more fatalities have occurred in the preceding three calendar years. Remedial Engineering Measures Immediate short term interventions: High visibility thermoplastic road markings, rumble strips before hazardous junctions, retro reflective cautionary signage, and electronic speed display boards. Medium to long term interventions: Junction geometric redesign, construction of vehicular underpasses (VUP) or pedestrian underpasses (PUP), installation of W beam crash barriers, and grade separated intersections. Maharashtra has identified over 450 black spots on state and national highways within the state as of 2022. 2. Speed Management Guidelines on National & State Highways Design Speed Limits: Access controlled expressways: 120 km/h for light motor vehicles (LMVs), 80 km/h for heavy commercial vehicles (HCVs). 4 lane divided National Highways: 100 km/h for LMVs, 80 km/h for HCVs. Undivided 2 lane State Highways: 70 km/h for LMVs, 60 km/h for HCVs. Urban arterial roads and school zones: 40 km/h and 25 km/h respectively. Enforcement Mechanisms: Sectional speed detection cameras over 5 km intervals rather than single point radar guns to discourage sudden braking. Maharashtra Traffic Police uses Interceptor vehicle mounted LIDAR guns for mobile speed enforcement on expressways. 3. Monsoon & Adverse Weather Safety Mandates Drainage and Skid Resistance: All highway concessionaires must inspect longitudinal drains before June 1 annually. Minimum skid resistance value of 55 BPN (British Pendulum Number) required on wet pavement surfaces. text: Repair Timelines: Potholes emerging on National Highway networks must be filled with cold mix or mastic asphalt within 48 hours of detection during rainy periods. During June September monsoon season, Maharashtra typically sees a 30 35% spike in road accident fatalities compared to dry months due to skidding on wet roads and reduced visibility. 4. Maharashtra Specific Accident Corridors Mumbai Pune Expressway (NH 48): Among the highest accident density expressways. Common causes: overspeeding, fog patches in Khandala Ghat section, tire burst. Nashik Pune Highway (NH 60): Significant truck LMV collision corridor. Nagpur Amravati Yavatmal Corridor: High fatality rate among Vidarbha region roads due to unlit stretches. Satara Kolhapur (NH 48 South): Frequent accidents at Karad bypass junctions. 5. Fatality Classification per MoRTH 6. Risk Score Computation Methodology (MoRTH Research Wing) MoRTH affiliated research institutions use composite risk scoring: Accident Severity Index (ASI): (3 × Fatal + 1 × Serious + 0.3 × Minor) / Total Accidents Accident Rate per MVKM: (Number of accidents / Vehicle Kilometers Traveled) × 10^6 Locations scoring 3 on ASI and 0.5 accidents/MVKM are classified as high priority intervention zones.
